claims.text: Premelting and melting behavior of HEA nanoparticles is mainly governed by high configurational entropy.
High configurational entropy drives selective surface segregation in HEA nanoparticles.
Selective surface segregation and local lattice strain narrow the free-energy gap between solid and liquid states.
Surface atomic disorder delays surface premelting relative to chemically simpler alloy nanoparticles.
High-entropy alloys contain at least five constituent metals.
Atomic-size diversity produces local lattice-strain fields in HEA nanoparticles.
High configurational entropy promotes a nonuniform surface distribution of constituent elements.
Selective segregation creates localized regions of elevated lattice strain.
Localized lattice strain enhances interatomic bonding at the nanoparticle surface.
Enhanced surface bonding and a reduced solid-liquid free-energy differential delay surface premelting and overall melting.
Matched HEA nanoparticles will exhibit higher premelting-onset temperatures than binary or ternary nanoparticles.
Matched HEA nanoparticles will melt several tens of kelvin above comparable binary or ternary nanoparticles.
The proposed effect should occur over a nanoparticle size range of 5–50 nm.
The proposed effect should hold for compositions with at least five principal elements and substantial mixing entropy.
The relative contributions of surface strain and segregation may depend on synthesis method and nanoparticle morphology.
Carbon-support interactions can thermally stabilize metallic nanoparticles by anchoring them to defective turbostratic graphite.
